Parents who choose Sharvash usually hope their child will grow to embody lord of auspiciousness and live with faith, good character and purpose.

data.cultural_impact: The name Sharvash carries significant cultural importance in Hinduism, as it references the revered Hindu deity Sharva. Sharva is believed to be the god of auspiciousness, fertility, and well-being. He is also known as the god of loyal friends and is often invoked for success, good luck, and positive change. Naming a child Sharvash would imbue them with these positive associations and blessings.
data.spiritual_significance: Spiritually, the name Sharvash signifies the embodiment of positivity, good fortune, and prosperity. It is a name that evokes the blessings of the Hindu deity Sharva and resonates with the divine energies of creation, abundance, and well-being. By carrying this name, an individual is reminded of the divine power within to manifest positive change, attract auspiciousness, and flourish in all areas of life.
data.spiritual_symbolism: Sharvash: Radiating the divine wisdom and grace of Lord Shiva. A beacon of spiritual knowledge and enlightenment.

historical_references.reference: Sharva is considered to be an incarnation of Shiva and is also known as Sharvani or Sharvashcharya. He is mentioned in various Hindu scriptures, including the Shiva Purana and the Skanda Purana. In the Shiva Purana, Sharva is described as the son of the goddess Parvati and is the elder brother of Kartikeya. He is also said to be the lord of all the Snakes and the patron of knowledge and learning.
historical_references.time_period: Ancient India, circa 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE

historical_references.reference: Another reference to Sharvash can be found in the Mahabharata, where he is mentioned as the father of the Pandava prince Bhima. Bhima, who was granted the boon of irresistible strength, angered the sage Vyasa by trying to abduct his daughter Satyavati. In retaliation, Vyasa cursed Bhima to be born as a monster, which was later mitigated by Sharvash, who intervened and asked Vyasa to restore Bhima to his original form. This episode is recounted in the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata.
